tip: Add -ach to an adjective to mean more. ‘doeth’ (wise) gives ‘doethach’; ‘yn’ then softens it to ‘ddoethach’ here, wiser.
‘yn’ before a noun softens its first letter. ‘cogydd’ (cook) becomes ‘gogydd’ in ‘mae e'n gogydd’.
Need uses ‘angen’ with ‘ar’. ‘oes angen help arnoch chi’ means do you need help, help on you.
‘yn fawr’ after ‘hoffi’ means a lot. ‘hoffi wyau yn fawr’ means like eggs very much.
Welsh normally starts with the verb. ‘mae'n gymylog’ means it is cloudy, the verb ‘mae’ coming first.
‘ar ôl’ here means left or remaining. ‘oes tocynnau ar ôl’ means are there tickets left.
A feminine noun softens its adjective. ‘noswaith’ is feminine, so ‘da’ becomes ‘dda’ in ‘noswaith dda’.
Your wraps the noun: ‘eich’ or ‘'ch’ before, ‘chi’ after. ‘ydy'ch rhif ffôn chi’ means your phone number.
Some adjectives take ‘o’ for of. ‘falch o’ means proud of, as in ‘falch o fy nghanlyniadau’.
‘yn’ links a verb to make the present tense. ‘mae hi'n dal y trên’ means she catches (or is catching) the train.
‘o’ (from) triggers soft mutation. ‘Caerdydd’ becomes ‘Gaerdydd’ in ‘dod o Gaerdydd’.
‘os gwelwch yn dda’ means please, literally if you see well. It often ends a polite request.
Adjectives normally follow the noun in Welsh. ‘bore da’ is literally morning good, meaning good morning.
‘yn’ softens an adjective. ‘da’ becomes ‘dda’ after ‘yn’, as in ‘dw i'n dda’, I am fine.
‘yn’ also means in for places. ‘yn y banc bwyd’ means in the food bank, unlike the linking ‘'n’.
‘o'r gloch’ means o'clock, literally of the bell. ‘am un o'r gloch’ means at one o'clock.
In south Wales possession uses ‘gyda’. ‘oes gyda chi frawd’ means do you have a brother.
A question inside a sentence keeps normal order. ‘ble mae'r amgueddfa’ means where the museum is.
‘eisiau’, to want, takes no ‘yn’ before it. ‘ydych chi eisiau diod’ means do you want a drink.
Feminine nouns normally soften after ‘y’. ‘tref’ (town) becomes ‘dref’ in ‘yn y dref’.
‘faint o’ means how many before a noun. ‘faint o fyfyrwyr’ means how many students.
The ending -odd marks past for he or she. ‘caodd hi’ means she closed.
Negatives add ‘ddim’. ‘dyw e ddim yn gwybod’ means he does not know, ‘dyw’ being negative ‘mae’.
Two has genders: ‘dau’ for masculine, ‘dwy’ for feminine. ‘chwaer’ is feminine, so ‘dwy chwaer’.
‘bydd’ is the future of ‘bod’ for he/she/it. Add ‘yn’ before the verb: ‘bydd y siop yn cau’ (the shop will close).
The number ‘dau’ softens the next noun. ‘tocyn’ becomes ‘docyn’ in ‘dau docyn’, two tickets.
‘mor’ plus ‘â’ means as ... as. ‘mor dal â'i dad’ means as tall as his father.
‘neu’ (or) triggers soft mutation. ‘caws’ (cheese) becomes ‘gaws’ in ‘bara neu gaws’.
‘na’ (than) triggers aspirate mutation on p, t, c. ‘pawb’ becomes ‘phawb’ in ‘na phawb’.
‘oes’ asks if something exists, ‘ydy’ asks about a known thing. ‘oes signal ffôn da yma’ means is there phone signal here.
